learning_objective: 🎯 Examine the dual nature of interviews: why celebrities despise them as unwarranted intrusions, and why journalists see them as the ultimate source of truth.

key_vocabulary.hindi_meaning: अभूतपूर्व (जो पहले कभी न हुआ हो)

main_concepts.concept_title: 🎙️ Part 1: The Dark Side of Interviews
main_concepts.simple_explanation: Many famous writers hate being interviewed. Lewis Carroll had a 'just horror of the interviewer', V.S. Naipaul feels people are 'wounded' by them, and Rudyard Kipling called it immoral, cowardly, and a crime.

Despite the hatred from celebrities, the interview is a supremely serviceable medium of communication. The interviewer holds a position of unprecedented power and influence because they extract the truth for the public.

Mukund Padmanabhan interviews Umberto Eco, a brilliant academic scholar who suddenly became a famous novelist with his book 'The Name of the Rose'. Eco is humble and cooperative, unlike the writers in Part 1.
When asked how he does so much work, Eco reveals his secret: he works in the 'interstices' (empty spaces). For example, he writes an article in the 10 minutes he waits for an elevator to come up.

Eco identifies himself as an academic scholar who attends academic conferences, not a novelist. He writes novels only on Sundays. 'The Name of the Rose' sold 10-15 million copies, but he remains grounded.

fun_activity.title: ⏳ Using the Interstices
fun_activity.instructions: Umberto Eco works in his 'empty spaces'. Next time you are waiting for a bus or the microwave to beep, use that 2 minutes to learn one new word or plan your day. That's an interstice!

exam_tips: 📌 Understand the paradox in Part 1: Celebrities hate interviews (calling it an assault on their privacy), but it remains the most powerful and widely read medium of journalism.
📌 Explain Eco's writing style: Unlike boring academic papers, Eco writes in a narrative, playful, and informal style that makes his scholarly work highly readable.

📌 Why was 'The Name of the Rose' so successful? Even Eco admits it's a mystery. It offered a serious, difficult reading experience at exactly the right time when publishers thought people only wanted trash.
quick_recap: ⭐ Saul Bellow described interviews as 'thumbprints on his windpipe'.
⭐ Eco wrote his doctoral dissertation by telling the story of his research (including his trials and errors), rather than just giving the final conclusion.
⭐ The chapter shows a stark contrast between authors who view interviews as a curse and Eco, who uses it brilliantly to explain his philosophy.
